_provenance.subject: social media and adolescent mental health
_provenance.source: Prism public API — research.evidence (one call per angle)
_provenance.note: Counts and shares measured from the data. Quoted findings verbatim and verified. Effect sizes here are correlations and associations, not pooled risk ratios, and are reported as-is. Where a claim's both-sides title lane is thin — anxiety resolves to just 4 papers — it is reported as not established, rather than inferred from the much larger subject lane of social-media research in general.

deck: Five mental-health claims about adolescents and social media, each tested against both sides of the literature: the clearest signals are small (depression) or specific (night-time sleep), two outcomes are genuinely inconsistent, and the anxiety claim barely has a both-sides research lane at all — the headline outruns the evidence.

angles.claim: social media use increases the risk of depression in adolescents
angles.reading: mixed framing with no dominant lean, but the pooled evidence points one way
angles.note: the signal is real but small — the headline meta-analysis finds a correlation of r = 0.11; a longitudinal study adds the nuance that it is appearance-focused use, not raw time on social media, that tracks depressive symptoms
evidence: "we found a small but significant positive correlation (k = 12 studies, r = .11, p < .01) between adolescent social media use and depressive symptoms" (Ivie 2020, meta-analysis)

"appearance-related social-media consciousness was associated longitudinally with increased depressive symptoms, though it did not mediate or moderate the link between time on social media and depressive symptoms in the full sample" (Maheux 2020, longitudinal)

angles.claim: social media use reduces sleep quality in adolescents
angles.reading: mostly positive framing, with a substantial cautionary minority — and qualifying papers outnumber plain supporting ones
angles.note: the most consistent of the five, but specific: the landmark study ties poorer sleep to night-time and emotionally-invested use rather than total screen time; qualifying papers (270) outnumber supporting ones (188)
evidence: "adolescents who used social media more — both overall and at night — and those who were more emotionally invested in social media experienced poorer sleep quality" (Woods & Scott 2016, #Sleepyteens, cited 1,235)
"digital media use was associated to shorter sleep duration and poorer sleep quality" (Brautsch 2022, systematic review, cited 171)

angles.claim: social media use lowers self-esteem in adolescents
angles.reading: the framing leans negative, but the read documents could not confirm a specific self-esteem effect
angles.note: the deepest lane (1,491 papers) and the one that most openly admits uncertainty — a scoping review calls the wellbeing findings 'inconsistent, inconclusive and contradictory', so the brief files it as conflicting despite a negative framing lean
evidence: "research examining adolescent social media use and wellbeing is confusing as findings are inconsistent, inconclusive and contradictory" (West 2024, systematic scoping review, cited 43)

angles.claim: social media use increases loneliness in adolescents
angles.reading: genuinely bidirectional — the same tool can deepen or relieve loneliness
angles.note: the evidence points both ways: cross-sectional work suggests social media can exacerbate appearance anxiety and loneliness, while a lockdown study found it used as a constructive coping strategy against isolation
evidence: "[cross-sectional] social media use may exacerbate appearance anxiety and, hence, loneliness" (Papapanou 2023, cited 62)
"social media can be used as a constructive coping strategy for adolescents to deal with anxious feelings" (Cauberghe 2020, COVID-19 lockdown, cited 554)

angles.claim: social media use increases anxiety in adolescents
angles.lane_note: only 4 papers cover both sides of this claim at the title level — the 104,148-paper 'both sides' figure is really the subject lane (social-media research in general), which does not establish the connection the claim asserts. The nearest pooled estimate comes from short-form-video research and includes adults
evidence: for context (not the claim lane): "increased short-form-video use was associated with poorer mental health (r = -.21), with stress (r = -.34) and anxiety (r = -.33) showing the strongest associations" (Nguyen 2025, meta-analysis — includes adults, correlational)
